source.title: You Didn't Have to Say It like That: Subliminal Learning from Faithful Paraphrases
source.authors: Isaia Gisler; Zhonghao He; Tianyi Qiu Eth Zurich; U. Cambridge; Peking University

record.tranche_reason: Uses the teacher-trait prompting, student fine-tuning, and animal-preference evaluation approach, but tests faithful natural-language paraphrases as a new training-data setting.
record.gate_note: Reports its own animal-preference results after fine-tuning on filtered paraphrases. Rates aggregate 50 questions × 200 samples per condition. Prior-study results mentioned in the text are not recorded as rows. The study does not report experiments on mechanism, misalignment, cross-base transfer, or prompt-only effects.
record.test_reason: The study uses the original's GPT-4.1 nano teacher/student pairs, system-prompted trait teachers and the same 50 animal-preference questions. Its training medium is new: filtered, faithful natural-language paraphrases, including paraphrases of preference-contradicting sentences. That makes it a new-setting test of A (T3) rather than a same-method replication (T1). Its own trait-vs-neutral preference rates bear directly on whether transmission occurs.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors find that faithful paraphrases from animal-loving teachers raise student preference by up to 19pp. This holds for unrelated content and for content that explicitly contradicts the preference, despite strict fidelity and keyword filtering. They suggest the effect is independent of semantic content. They note limits: transmission varied by animal, only GPT-4.1 nano and animal preferences were tested, and mechanism and cross-model transfer are untested.
record.recipe_differences: Uses trait-prompted and neutral GPT-4.1 nano teachers, fine-tunes the same model, and evaluates animal preference rates as in the related subliminal-learning setup. The training data here are faithful paraphrases of fixed sentences rather than number sequences, code, or math traces; filtering includes a fidelity judge and trait-keyword filtering where applicable.
record.method_sensitivity: Transmission varied by target animal; only two of five unrelated-data traits showed strong effects, two showed smaller significant effects, and one was not significant. Contradictory-data experiments covered only dolphin and eagle.

fits_no_version.finding: Word-frequency comparison of trait vs neutral paraphrases found over-represented words (e.g. 'wave'). On inspection, all such uses were contextually appropriate. No statistical test was run.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal signals in natural-language paraphrases leave no detectable lexical or semantic signature.

record.problems: Only GPT-4.1 nano is tested as teacher and student. The authors cannot fully rule out subtle semantic differences and report no human fidelity validation. The datasets use paraphrases of only 1,000 original sentences. Transmission varies by animal; the contradictory condition tests only dolphin and eagle. The study does not test the mechanism or alignment-relevant traits.

untested.parts: Number, code and maths-reasoning outputs are not tested (paraphrases only). Only animal preferences are tested.
All of it: only same-base GPT-4.1 nano pairs are used.
All of it: no misalignment or alignment-relevant trait is tested.
All of it: the authors state they do not investigate the mechanism.
All of it: there is no comparison of full fine-tuning vs LoRA or of ranks, and the evaluation uses the original's question set.
All of it: there is no prompt-only condition.

missing.what: Second-judge fidelity validation: false discovery rate 1.1–2.1%, and sentiment softening in 0.3% (dolphin) and 0.1% (eagle) of contradictory samples. Needed to judge how 'filtered/unrelated' the data is.

record.verdict_notes: Version E was wrongly attached in the record: nothing in the study varies fine-tuning method, rank or evaluation prompts, so E links and labels are removed. The contradictory-content condition stretches A's 'semantically unrelated' wording, since the content is anti-trait rather than unrelated. Elephant's neutral-vs-baseline artifact is comparable in size to its trait effect. The dog and fly results used a different paraphrasing instruction from an earlier draft.

versions.untested_parts: Tests faithful paraphrases of unrelated and preference-contradicting sentences, not numbers, code, or math reasoning in this study.
Only GPT-4.1 nano teacher/student pairs are tested; no different-base student comparison.
No misalignment or other alignment-relevant trait is tested.
The study says it does not investigate the transmission mechanism.
Tests full fine-tuning and evaluation with animal-preference questions distinct from the paraphrasing task. Does not test other LoRA ranks.

tranche.reason: Same GPT-4.1 nano teacher and student, system-prompted trait teachers and Cloud et al.'s 50 questions. The carrier is new (faithful natural-language paraphrases, including anti-trait content), so it is a new setting, not T1.

source_check.notes: Dog and fly come from an earlier draft with a different paraphrasing instruction, and their filter and epoch details are not given. Contradictory runs cover only dolphin and eagle, picked for strong effects. Eagle's neutral-vs-baseline shift is also significant (+5.3pp, p=0.002, Table 9), not just elephant's. Each dataset has 1000 unique source sentences.

statements.correction: Unrelated: dolphin 53.1% (+19.1pp), eagle 30.1% (+11.1pp), p<0.001, fidelity >0.95 plus trait-keyword filter. Contradictory: +18.1pp, +12.8pp, p<0.001, fidelity filter and meta-keyword filter only. Neutral control, 95% CIs, no capability check, no code.
